gap: No result ChatGPT got states that 60 kW of continuous output is out of reach on a US home's 120/240 V service. EcoFlow's DELTA Pro Ultra tops out at 21.6 kW from three units and the DELTA Pro Ultra X at 36 kW from three. Anker's SOLIX E10 tops out at 22.8 kW continuous (30 kW turbo for 90 minutes) from three units on one Power Dock. The only 60 kW unit ChatGPT showed, the Sol-Ark 60K-3P-480V, is a 277/480 V three-phase commercial inverter that needs its own 300 V+ battery bank.
standout_why: I compared against the cited EcoFlow pages. The DELTA Pro Ultra X specs page (ecoflow.com/us/delta-pro-ultra-x/specs) states 'Up to 36kW in 3 parallel units', and the DELTA Pro Ultra pages state '21.6kW Max (Three Units)'. So the per-brand ceiling is already partly covered by a cited rival. None of ChatGPT's 30 results compares any product against 60 kW. None states the Anker E10 ceiling (Anker was a card, but no Anker page was in its results). None of its results states that the 60 kW Sol-Ark is native 277/480 V three-phase only and needs a separate 300 V+ battery. ChatGPT's own answer only says 'likely need a professionally designed multi-inverter system', which never explains why.
decides: If the shopper means 60 kW of output, no 120/240 V home-backup system in this category can deliver it. The best is EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra X at 36 kW with three inverters. A true 60 kW unit means a commercial three-phase 277/480 V site, not a house. Arithmetic, not a sourced figure: 60,000 W at 240 V is 250 A, which is more than a typical 200 A home main panel can carry. If the shopper means 60 kWh of storage, a single DELTA Pro Ultra X inverter reaches it (61.44 kWh). This confirms ChatGPT's 'pick a unit' question and points the 60 kWh reading to the DPU X.
